Grand Duke [Jiāng] said:
"In all matters of rewards, trustworthiness is valued;
in all matters of punishments, certainty is valued.
If rewards are trustworthy and punishments are certain in what is heard and seen,
then what is not heard and seen will inevitably be transformed in secret.
For sincerity penetrates heaven and earth,
and communicates with the spirits,
how much more so with people?"
*The Way of Warfare*
King Wǔ asked Grand Duke [Jiāng], saying:
"What is the way of warfare like?"
Grand Duke [Jiāng] said:
"In all matters of the way of warfare,
nothing surpasses 'one'.
'One' means to be able to go alone and come alone.
"The Yellow Emperor said:
'One' is a step towards the Dao,
bordering on the divine.
Its use lies in opportunity,
its manifestation lies in momentum,
its success lies in the ruler.
"Therefore, the sage kings call weapons inauspicious instruments,
and only use them when there is no alternative.
"Now the King of Shāng knows only of existence and does not know of ruin,
Knowing joy but not knowing disaster.
That which exists is not truly existing,
but lies in considering loss.
Joy is not truly joy,
but lies in considering disaster.
Now that Your Majesty has already considered its source,
how could you worry about its outflow?"
Wǔ Wáng 武王 said:
"When two armies meet,
they cannot come,
we cannot go,
each sets up firm defenses,
not daring to strike first.
I wish to attack them by surprise,
but cannot gain an advantage,
what should be done about it?"
Tài Gōng 太公 said:
"Appear outwardly disordered but be inwardly disciplined,
appear hungry but be actually full,
be inwardly keen but outwardly dull,
sometimes united, sometimes separated,
sometimes gathered, sometimes scattered,
conceal your plans,
keep your strategies secret;
build your ramparts high,
hide your sharp forces.
"The soldiers should be as silent as if nonexistent,
so the enemy will not know our preparations.
Pretend to attack in the west,
and strike in the east."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"If the enemy knows our situation
and understands our plans,
what should be done?"
Tàigōng said:
"The art of winning battles lies in
secretly observing the enemy's vulnerabilities and quickly capitalizing on their weaknesses,
then swiftly attacking where they least expect it."
Wǔ Tāo
"Fā Qǐ"
When Wén Wáng was in Fēng,
he summoned Tàigōng and said:
"Alas!
The King of Shāng is extremely tyrannical,
killing the innocent without cause.
Gōng Shàng, assist me in worrying about the people.
What should we do?"
Tàigōng said:
"Your Majesty, cultivate virtue,
show kindness to the worthy and bestow favor on the people,
in order to observe the Way of Heaven.
The Way of Heaven is without calamity;
one should not take the initiative to usher it in.
The Way of Man is without disaster;
one should not take the initiative to scheme for it.
Only when one surely sees the calamity of Heaven,
and also sees the disaster of Man,
then can one scheme.
Only when one surely sees its bright side (*yáng*),
and also sees its dark side (*yīn*),
then can one know its heart.
Only when one surely sees its exterior,
and also sees its interior,
then can one know its intent.
Only when one surely sees its estrangement,
and also sees its closeness,
then can one know its feelings.
"Follow its Way,
and the Way can be attained.
Go through its door,
and the door can be entered.
Establish its rites,
and the rites can be accomplished.
Contend for its strength,
and the strength can be overcome.
"Complete victory without fighting,
a great army without wounds,
communicating with spirits and gods—
How subtle!
How subtle!
"Sharing benefits with others,
sympathizing with and helping each other in sickness,
nurturing each other with mutual understanding,
assisting each other in hating evil,
and converging in shared preferences."
"Therefore, one can win without armor and weapons,
attack without siege engines,
and defend without moats and ramparts."
"The greatest wisdom is not wisdom;
the greatest planning is not planning;
the greatest courage is not courage;
the greatest benefit is not benefit."
"He who benefits the world,
the world will open to him;
he who harms the world,
the world will close to him."
The world is not one person's world,
but the world's world.
"To take the world is like chasing a wild beast;
if captured, everyone desires to share the meat.
It is like crossing a river in the same boat;
if successful, all share the benefits;
if defeated, all share the harm."
If they fail, they will all share in the harm.
Therefore, everything should be opened up,
and nothing should be closed off.
"He who takes nothing from the people,
gains the people;
he who takes nothing from the state,
gains the state;
he who takes nothing from all under Heaven,
gains all under Heaven."
"He who takes nothing from the people,
the people benefit from him;
he who takes nothing from the state,
the state benefits from him;
he who takes nothing from all under Heaven,
all under Heaven benefits from him."
"Therefore, the Dao is in the invisible,
the affairs are in the unheard,
the victory is in the unknowable.
Subtle indeed!
Subtle indeed!
When a bird of prey is about to strike,
it flies low and folds its wings;
when a fierce beast is about to pounce,
it flattens its ears and crouches low;
when a sage is about to act,
he must show a semblance of foolishness."
"Now, regarding that Yīn Shāng,
the multitude is deluded by each other's words.
They are in utter chaos and confusion,
their lust for indulgence knows no bounds;
this is a sign of a state's demise.
"When I observe their fields,
weeds and reeds surpass the grain.
When I observe their people,
crookedness surpasses uprightness.
When I observe their officials,
they are violent, tyrannical, and cruel.
They ruin laws and disorder punishments,
those above and below are unaware.
This is the time of a state's demise.
"When great light shines forth, all things are illuminated;
when great righteousness arises, all things benefit;
when great armies are mobilized, all things submit.
How great is
the virtue of the sage!
He alone hears and sees clearly,
how joyful!"
*Wén Qǐ*
Wén Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"What does a sage guard?"
Tài Gōng said,
"Without worry or stinginess,
All things can be obtained;
why be stingy, why worry?
All things are vigorous.
"Where governance is applied,
no one knows how it transforms;
where the times are,
no one knows how it shifts.
The sage guards this, and all things transform.
What limit is there?
Ending and beginning again.
"Relax and roam freely.
Seek it diligently;
having sought and obtained it,
it must not be hidden.
Having hidden it,
it must not fail to be acted upon;
having acted upon it,
do not explain it again."
"Now, Heaven and Earth do not illuminate themselves,
therefore they can live long;
the sage does not illuminate himself,
therefore his name becomes manifest."
"The ancient sages,
gathered people to form families,
gathered families to form states,
gathered states to form all under Heaven.
They enfeoffed virtuous men to establish myriad states,
and called this "Dà Jì" (Great Record).
"They displayed their policies and teachings,
accommodated their people's customs,
transformed the crooked into the straight,
and changed their appearance.
The myriad states did not interact,
each enjoyed their own place,
and the people loved their superiors.
This was called "Dà Dìng" (Great Stability).
"Alas!
The sage strives for tranquility,
the worthy man strives for uprightness;
the foolish man cannot be upright,
therefore he contends with others.
If the ruler is weary, punishments will be numerous;
if punishments are numerous, the people will be worried;
if the people are worried, they will flee.
If superiors and inferiors are not at peace in their lives,
and the toil continues for generations,
this is called "Dà Shī" (Great Loss).
"The people of the world are like flowing water:
block it and it stops,
open it and it flows,
stir it and it becomes muddy,
leave it still and it becomes clear.
Alas!
How divine!
When a sage observes the beginning,
he knows its end."
Wén Wáng said:
"How can one achieve stillness?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Heaven has a constant form,
and the people have a constant life.
Share life with the world,
and the world will be at peace.
The highest ruler follows it,
the next best transforms it.
For the people are transformed and follow governance.
Therefore, Heaven accomplishes things through non-action,
and the people become wealthy without being involved.
This is the virtue of a sage."
Wén Wáng said:
"Your words, Sir, are in accordance with my thoughts,
I will remember them day and night without forgetting,
and use them as a constant guide."
*Wén Fá* (Civil Conquest)
Wén Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"What is the method of civil conquest?"
Tài Gōng said:
In general, there are twelve principles of employing literary warfare:
One:
Cater to what they like,
and comply with their desires.
When they become arrogant,
they will surely indulge in pleasures.
If you can capitalize on this,
you will surely be able to remove them.
Two:
Befriend those they love,
to diminish their authority.
When one person has divided loyalties,
their power will surely decline.
If the court has no loyal ministers,
the state will surely be in danger.
Three:
Secretly bribe their attendants,
to gain deep insights into their situation.
When secrets within become known without,
the state will suffer harm.
Four:
Assist their extravagant pleasures,
to expand their ambitions.
Offer lavish bribes of pearls and jade,
entertain them with beautiful women.
Use humble words and submissive listening,
Conform to fate and unite.
If they do not contend,
treacherous schemes will then be settled.
"Fifth:
Treat their loyal ministers with strictness,
and reduce their bribes,
detain their envoys,
and do not listen to their affairs.
Quickly appoint replacements for them,
present them with sincere matters,
treat them with intimacy and trust,
and their ruler will again unite with you.
If you can be strict with them,
their state can then be plotted against.
"Sixth:
Gather their internal affairs,
and sow discord externally.
When talented ministers become external prime ministers,
and enemy states invade internally,
few states will not perish.
"Seventh:
If you wish to solidify their hearts,
you must heavily bribe them.
Gather their loyal and loving attendants,
secretly show them benefits,
cause them to belittle their endeavors,
And the accumulated stores will be emptied.
"Eighth:
Bribe them with heavy treasures,
and then conspire with them.
Conspire and benefit them,
if they benefit, they will surely trust,
this is called repeated affection.
The accumulation of repeated affection
will surely be used by me.
If they possess a state abroad,
its territory will be greatly defeated.
"Ninth:
Honor them with a title,
do not make things difficult for them;
show them the great power,
following it will surely be believed;
give them great respect,
first bring them glory,
subtly adorn them as sages,
and the state will be greatly stolen.
"Tenth:
Humble yourself to them, and they will surely trust,
in order to obtain their true feelings.
Receive their intentions and respond to events,
as if you share the same life.
Having already obtained it,
then subtly gather it in.
When the time is about to arrive,
act as if heaven is bereaving him.
"Section Eleven says:
'Choke it with the Way':
No subject of a ruler does not value high position and wealth,
and detest death and blame.
Subtly display great respect,
and secretly transfer heavy treasures,
to gather its outstanding talents;
internally accumulate greatly,
while externally feigning inadequacy;
secretly admit wise scholars,
and have them devise plans;
admit brave warriors,
and let them elevate their spirit;
let wealth and honor be exceedingly sufficient,
and constantly have abundant increase;
when followers are already prepared,
this is called choking it.
Having a state and choking it,
how can one possess the state?
"Section Twelve says:
'Nourish his rebellious ministers to confuse him,
present beautiful women and lewd music to bewilder him,
Abandon good dogs and horses to exhaust them;
use the times and the general situation to entice them;
the ruler observes [the situation above],
and plans with the world.
"When the twelve segments are complete,
martial affairs are then accomplished.
The so-called observing Heaven above,
observing Earth below,
verifying what has been seen,
then attacking."
*Shùn Qǐ*
Wén Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"How can one govern the world?"
Tài Gōng said,
"One must cover the world with generosity,
then one can accommodate the world;
one must cover the world with trustworthiness,
then one can bind the world;
one must cover the world with benevolence,
then one can cherish the world;
one must cover the world with kindness,
then one can protect the world;
one must cover the world with authority,
then one can avoid losing the world.
If actions are without doubt,
then the movements of Heaven cannot be shifted,
and the changes of time cannot be altered.
When these six are complete,
then one can govern the world.
"Therefore, one who benefits the world,
the world will open to him;
one who harms the world,
the world will shut him out;
one who gives life to the world,
the world will be grateful to him;
one who kills the world,
the world will be a bandit to him;
one who removes obstacles for the world,
the world will connect with him;
one who impoverishes the world,
the world will hate him;
one who brings peace to the world,
the world will rely on him;
one who endangers the world,
the world will bring disaster upon him.
The world is not one person's world,
only the one with the Dao can possess it."
*Sān Yí* (Three Doubts)
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"I wish to establish merit,
but I have three doubts:
I fear my strength will not be able to overcome the strong,
alienate relatives,
Dispersing the multitude,
how should it be done?"
Tàigōng said:
"Take advantage of them,
plan cautiously,
use wealth.
To attack the strong,
you must nourish them to make them strong,
increase them to make them expand.
Too strong will surely break,
too expanded will surely crack.
"Attack strength with strength,
separate relatives with relatives,
scatter the multitude with the multitude.
"Generally, the way of planning
is to value thoroughness and secrecy.
Engage them with affairs,
amuse them with profit,
a competitive spirit will surely arise.
"If you want to separate their relatives,
take advantage of what they love,
give to their favorites,
give them what they desire,
show them what is profitable,
and then alienate them,
Do not allow them to achieve their ambition.
If they are exceedingly delighted by greed for profit,
Abandon your doubts, and then stop.
"Generally, the way to attack is
one must first block their intelligence,
and then attack their strength, destroy their greatness,
and eliminate the people's harm.
"Indulge them with beauty,
entice them with profit,
nourish them with delicacies,
entertain them with pleasure.
"Once they are separated from their relatives,
be sure to alienate the people,
and do not let them know the plans.
Support them and lead them in,
so that no one perceives their intention,
and then it can be accomplished.
"Bestow favors on the people,
and be sure not to begrudge your wealth.
Treat the people like cattle and horses,
feed them frequently,
and then love them.
"The mind is used to enlighten wisdom,
wisdom is used to enlighten wealth,
wealth is used to enlighten the masses,
They all enlightened the worthy.
The possession of the worthy who are enlightened
is how one rules the world."
*Lóng Tāo*
"Wang Yi"
King Wu asked Tàigōng, saying:
"When a king leads an army,
he must have trusted aides, limbs and wings, to establish awe-inspiring divine power.
What should he do to accomplish this?"
Tàigōng said:
"Whenever raising troops and leading an army,
the general is the lifeblood.
The lifeblood lies in thorough understanding,
not adhering to a single tactic.
Assign duties according to ability,
each taking what they are best at,
adapting to change at all times,
and using this as the guiding principle.
"Therefore, a general should have seventy-two trusted aides, limbs and wings,
to correspond to the Way of Heaven.
Have a complete number according to the law,
carefully understand the principles of fate.
With various skills and unique abilities,
all matters will be completed."
King Wu said:
"May I ask about their categories?"
Tàigōng said:
"One confidant:
Primarily responsible for secret planning and responding to emergencies,
assessing the heavens and eliminating changes,
overseeing all plans and strategies,
and protecting the lives of the people.
"Five strategists:
Primarily responsible for planning for security and danger,
anticipating the unsprouted,
discussing conduct and ability,
clarifying rewards and punishments,
assigning official positions,
resolving suspicions,
and deciding what is permissible and impermissible.
"Three astronomers:
Primarily responsible for overseeing the stars and calendar,
observing the wind conditions,
calculating times and dates,
examining signs and verifications,
investigating calamities and anomalies,
and understanding the mechanisms of popular sentiment's movement and direction.
"Three geographers:
Primarily responsible for the army's movements and formations,
beneficial and harmful news,
distances, dangers, and ease of access,
water depletion and mountain blockages,
Not losing the advantage of terrain.
"The *Bīngfǎ* (military strategy) Nine Men:
Mainly discussing similarities and differences,
Success and failure of actions,
Simplifying and refining weapons,
Pointing out and punishing illegal activities.
"The Supply Four Men:
Mainly managing food and drink, storage,
Keeping supply routes open,
Delivering the five grains,
So that the three armies are not in distress.
"The Valiant Four Men:
Mainly selecting talent and strength,
Discussing weapons and armor,
Moving swiftly like wind and lightning,
Their whereabouts unknown.
"The Drum and Flag Three Men:
Mainly controlling the drums and flags,
Sharpening ears and eyes,
Deceiving with tallies,
Falsifying orders,
Secretly and suddenly coming and going,
Appearing and disappearing like spirits.
"The Limbs Four Men:
Mainly taking on heavy responsibilities and enduring difficulties,
Repair ditches and moats,
Fortify walls and ramparts,
In order to prepare for defense.
"Three versatile talents:
Primarily to pick up omissions and make amends for faults,
Respond to occasional guests,
Debate and discuss matters,
Alleviate troubles and resolve conflicts.
"Three strategists:
Primarily to execute extraordinary strategies,
Devise unusual plans,
Beyond what ordinary people can comprehend,
Carry out limitless transformations.
"Seven eyes and ears:
Primarily to travel around,
Listen to opinions and observe changes,
Examine the affairs of the four directions,
And the state of affairs within the army.
"Five claws and teeth:
Primarily to display might and valor,
Inspire the three armies,
Making them brave dangers and attack with sharp resolve,
Without any doubts or hesitations.
"Four wings:
Primarily to spread fame and reputation,
Intimidate distant lands,
Shaking the four borders,
using weakness to undermine the enemy's resolve.
"Eight itinerant scholars:
They primarily observe treachery and await changes,
open and close (exploit) human feelings,
observe the enemy's intentions,
and act as spies.
"Two occultists:
They primarily practice deception,
relying on ghosts and spirits,
to confuse the minds of the masses.
"Two alchemists:
They primarily deal with all kinds of medicines,
to treat metal-inflicted wounds,
and to heal all kinds of diseases.
"Two mathematicians:
They primarily calculate the layout of the three armies' camps, provisions, and the income and expenditure of wealth and resources."
*Lùn Jiàng* (On Command)
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng, saying:
"What is the principle of commanding generals?"
Tài Gōng said:
"A general possesses five qualities and ten faults."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"May I ask what they are?"
Tàigōng said:
"The so-called five qualities are:
courage (yǒng), wisdom (zhì), benevolence (rén), trustworthiness (xìn), and loyalty (zhōng).
With courage, one cannot be violated;
with wisdom, one cannot be thrown into confusion;
with benevolence, one loves others;
with trustworthiness, one does not deceive others;
with loyalty, one has no divided heart.
"The so-called ten faults are:
having courage but treating death lightly;
being hurried but having a quick temper;
being greedy and fond of profit;
having benevolence but being unendurable to people;
having wisdom but being timid;
being trustworthy but delighting in trusting others;
being incorruptible but not loving people;
having wisdom but being slow in temperament;
being resolute but self-opinionated;
being weak but delighting in entrusting tasks to others.
"He who has courage but treats death lightly
can be treated with violence;
he who is hurried but has a quick temper
can be kept for a long time;
he who is greedy and fond of profit
can be abandoned;
he who has benevolence but is unendurable to people
can be toiled;
One who is intelligent but timid can be cornered;
One who is trustworthy and readily trusts others can be deceived;
One who is honest and pure but does not love people can be insulted;
One who is intelligent but slow-witted can be ambushed;
One who is resolute and self-reliant can be employed;
One who is cowardly but likes to entrust matters to others can be cheated.
Therefore, warfare is a major affair of the state,
the way to survival and destruction,
and destiny lies in the hands of the general.
The general is the support of the state,
valued by the former kings.
Therefore, the appointment of a general must be carefully considered.
Therefore, it is said:
Armies do not win twice,
nor do they lose twice.
When armies cross borders,
within ten days,
if there isn't a destroyed state,
there will certainly be a defeated army and a slain general.
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent."
*Xuǎn Jiàng* ("Selecting Generals")
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"When a ruler raises an army,
and wishes to select and train heroes,
and know the rank and ability of his officers,
what should be done?"
Tài Gōng said,
"There are fifteen ways in which an officer's outward appearance does not correspond to their inner feelings:
There are those who are stern but unworthy;
there are those who are gentle and kind but are thieves;
there are those who appear respectful but are arrogant at heart;
there are those who are outwardly upright but lack inner sincerity;
there are those who are energetic but without compassion;
there are those who are profound but without honesty;
there are those who are good at planning but indecisive;
there are those who seem bold but are incapable;
there are those who are empty-headed but untrustworthy;
there are those who are dazed and confused but are actually loyal and sincere;
there are those who are unconventional and extreme but effective;
there are those who are outwardly brave but inwardly timid;
there are those who are solemn but easily changed by others;
there are those who are harsh but actually calm and honest;
there are those who appear weak and insignificant but go everywhere and accomplish everything.
"What the world despises,
the sage values;
Ordinary people do not know this;
without great discernment, one cannot see the disparity.
This refers to a person whose outward appearance does not match their inner feelings."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"How does one know this?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Knowing them involves eight signs:
First, question them with words to observe their rhetoric.
Second, press them with arguments to observe their adaptability.
Third, involve them in private consultations to observe their sincerity.
Fourth, ask them clear and direct questions to observe their virtue.
Fifth, entrust them with wealth to observe their integrity.
Sixth, test them with beauty to observe their chastity.
Seventh, inform them of difficulties to observe their courage.
Eighth, intoxicate them with wine to observe their demeanor.
If all eight signs are present,
then the worthy and the unworthy will be distinguished."
《Lì Jiàng》
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng, saying:
"What is the way to establish a general?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Whenever the country faces a crisis,
the ruler should avoid the main hall,
summon the general and instruct him, saying:
'The safety and danger of the state
rests entirely on the general.
Now, a certain state is disobedient,
I wish the general to lead the army to respond to it.'
Once the general has received the order,
then order the grand historian to divine,
fast for three days,
go to the great ancestral temple,
drill the sacred tortoise shell,
divine for an auspicious day,
and bestow the axe and钺 [yuè].
The ruler enters the temple gate,
stands facing west;
the general enters the temple gate,
stands facing north.
The ruler personally holds the yuè [yuè],
holding its head,
and bestows its handle to the general,
saying:
'From here on out,
Those above, reaching to the heavens,
the general shall control them.”
He again grasped the axe,
holding its handle,
and presented its blade to the general,
saying:
“From here below,
down to the depths,
the general shall control them.
If you see their weakness,
then advance;
if you see their strength,
then halt.
Do not underestimate the enemy because your three armies are large,
do not deem death inevitable because you have received orders,
do not disdain others because of your own high status,
do not go against the crowd because of your own unique views,
do not assume that persuasive arguments are necessarily correct.
Do not sit until your soldiers have sat,
do not eat until your soldiers have eaten;
you must share the cold and heat with them.
If you do this,
then your soldiers will certainly exert their utmost strength to the death.”
Once the general has received the order,
he bows and reports to the ruler, saying:
“Your subject has heard that a state cannot be governed from the outside,
The army cannot be directed from the center.
A divided heart cannot serve a ruler,
a doubtful will cannot respond to the enemy.
Since your servant has received the command,
I wield the authority of the axe.
Your servant dares not return alive;
I wish Your Majesty would also bestow a single command upon your servant.
If Your Majesty does not permit your servant,
your servant dares not lead.”
The ruler permitted it,
and then he took his leave and departed.
“In matters of the army,
not hearing the ruler's commands,
all proceeds from the general.
When the general faces the enemy in decisive battle,
there can be no divided heart.
If this is so,
then there is no heaven above,
no earth below,
no enemy in front,
no ruler behind.
Therefore, the wise formulate plans for it,
the brave fight for it;
their spirit towers above the blue clouds,
swift as a galloping horse;
the soldiers do not even cross blades,
and the enemy surrenders and submits.
"Victory in battle abroad,
merit established at home.
Officials promoted, soldiers rewarded,
the people rejoice and are pleased,
the general will be without fault or misfortune.
Therefore, wind and rain will be timely,
the five grains will ripen abundantly,
and the state will be peaceful and tranquil."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent."
*General's Authority*
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"How does a general establish authority?
How does he establish clarity?
How does he establish thoroughness?
How does he establish prohibitions and ensure that orders are carried out?"
Tài Gōng said:
"A general establishes authority by punishing the great,
establishes clarity by rewarding the small;
establishes prohibitions and ensures that orders are carried out by making punishments thorough.
Therefore, if killing one person shakes the entire army,
kill him;
if killing one person makes ten thousand tremble,
kill him;
if killing one person makes ten million fear,
Kill them;
If rewarding one person causes ten thousand people to rejoice,
reward them.
Therefore, "Punishments should be weighted towards the great,
and rewards should be weighted towards the small.
Killing a prominent and esteemed minister who is in power
is the utmost in punishing superiors;
Rewarding cowherds, horse washers, and stable keepers
is allowing rewards to reach the lowest ranks.
Reaching the utmost in punishing superiors
and allowing rewards to reach the lowest ranks
is where the general's authority is exercised.
If killing one person goes unnoticed by the entire army,
if killing one person is unknown to the myriad people,
if killing one person does not frighten the millions and thousands,
even if many are killed,
the general's authority will not be weighty.

undefended locations,

set up signal fires for distant observation,

those who go out first

*Military Strategies*

there is no preparation of boats or bridges,

so that the three armies do not linger.

if instruction is not routinely trusted,

there is nothing that is not routinely practiced using equipment.

to observe inside the city,

for the three armies to advance and halt,

then there will be talented soldiers and powerful crossbows

if they cross large rivers,

if they go upstream against the current,

beat drums,

Dispatch my elite soldiers

attacking where they have no defenses.

to tire their minds;
order my old and weak

shouting and moving back and forth,

sometimes appearing from their right,

*Dòng Jìng* (Movement and Stillness)

amplify the sound of our gongs and drums.

let men hold banners,

cautiously guard the passes and bridges,

be carefully prepared and do not lose track of them,
the enemy will be fearful,

Brave and strong soldiers,

and the soldiers are confused.
I wish to be able to defend and be secure,
and to fight and be victorious.
What should I do?"
Tàigōng said:
"Whenever an army is stationed high on a mountain,
it becomes a roost for the enemy;
when stationed at the foot of a mountain,
it becomes a prisoner of the enemy.
Having settled against the mountain,
one must adopt the formation of a flock of birds.
The formation of a flock of birds
has both yin and yang prepared.
Some encamp on its shady side,
and some encamp on its sunny side.
If stationed on the sunny side of the mountain,
prepare against the shady side of the mountain;
if stationed on the shady side of the mountain,
prepare against the sunny side of the mountain.
If stationed to the left of the mountain,
prepare against the right of the mountain.
If stationed to the right of the mountain,
prepare against the left of the mountain.
If there are mountains that the enemy can climb,
deploy troops to defend their exterior.
Obstruct crossroads and valleys
with armored vehicles.
Place banners high;
I carefully instruct the entire army,
not to let the enemy know our situation.
This is called a mountain stronghold.
The ranks are already arranged,
the soldiers are already arrayed,
the laws and commands are already executed,
the surprise attacks and standard formations are already set up,
placing defensive positions on the exterior of the mountain,
in locations convenient for troops.
Then divide the chariots and cavalry into a "Bird Cloud" formation.
If the whole army fights fiercely,
even if the enemy is numerous,
their general can be captured."
*Niǎo Yún Zé Bīng* ("Bird Cloud Swamp Tactics")
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"Leading troops deep into the territory of the feudal lords,
and facing the enemy across the water.
The enemy is rich and numerous,
we are poor and few.
Crossing the water to attack them,
we cannot advance;
wanting to prolong the days,
our provisions are few.
We are stationed in barren, salty land,
with no settlements around,
and no grass or trees.
The army has nothing to plunder,
The cattle and horses have nothing to graze on.
What should be done about this?"
Tàigōng said:
"If the three armies are unprepared,
the cattle and horses have no food,
and the soldiers have no provisions,
then,
quickly deceive the enemy and quickly leave,
setting up an ambush behind."
King Wǔ said:
"The enemy cannot be deceived,
and my soldiers are confused.
If the enemy outflanks us front and rear,
and my three armies are defeated and flee in disorder,
what should be done about this?"
Tàigōng said:
"In seeking a way out,
gold and jade are the most important,
you must rely on enemy emissaries,
and subtlety is the treasure."
King Wǔ said:
"If the enemy knows of my ambush,
and the main army is unwilling to cross,
but separate generals divide their forces,
to cross the river,
and my three armies are greatly frightened,
"What should be done about it?"
Tàigōng said:
"In such a situation,
divide and form a rushing formation,
placing the troops where it is advantageous.
Wait until they have completely emerged,
then unleash my ambushed troops,
and quickly strike their rear.
Strong crossbows on both sides
should shoot their left and right flanks.
The chariots and cavalry should divide into a 'bird cloud' formation,
prepared for their front and rear.
The three armies should fight fiercely.
When the enemy sees us engaged in battle,
their main force will certainly cross the river to come.
Unleash my ambushed troops
to quickly strike their rear;
the chariots and cavalry should charge their left and right flanks.
Even if the enemy is numerous,
their general can be routed."
"The great principle of employing troops
when facing the enemy in battle
is to certainly employ a rushing formation,
placing the troops where it is advantageous.
Then use the army's cavalry to divide into a 'bird cloud' formation—
this is the key to using troops effectively.
"What is meant by 'bird cloud'
is that the birds scatter while the clouds gather,
resulting in endless changes."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent!"
*Shǎo Zhòng* (Less Versus Many)
Wǔ Wáng asked Tàigōng, saying:
"I wish to attack the many with the few,
and attack the strong with the weak.
How should I do it?"
Tàigōng said:
"To attack the many with the few,
it must be at the end of the day,
lying in ambush in deep grass,
intercepting them at a narrow pass.
To attack the strong with the weak,
you must obtain the support of a large state, or the assistance of a neighboring state."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"I have no deep grass,
nor do I have a narrow pass;
the enemy has already arrived,
it is not yet sunset;
I have no support from a large state,
nor do I have assistance from a neighboring state.
What should I do?"
Tàigōng said:
"[Use] false claims and deceptive inducements
to confuse their general.
Make their route circuitous,
causing them to pass through deep grass;
lengthen their road,
causing them to meet the sun-filled road.
When those in front have not yet crossed the water,
and those behind have not reached their quarters,
unleash my ambush troops,
quickly attacking their left and right flanks,
with chariots and cavalry disrupting their front and rear.
Even if the enemy is numerous,
their general can be made to flee."
"[When] serving the ruler of a large state,
be humble towards the officers of neighboring states.
Make your gifts generous,
and your words humble.
Doing this,
you will gain the support of the large state and the assistance of the neighboring states."
Wǔwáng said:
"Excellent."
*Fēn Xiǎn* (Dividing the Perilous)
Wǔwáng asked Tàigōng, saying:
"Leading troops deep into the territory of the feudal lords,
and encountering the enemy in a perilous and narrow place,
"We are on the left of the mountain and the right of the water,
while the enemy is on the right of the mountain and the left of the water,
using the natural defenses to oppose us.
I want to be secure if we defend,
and victorious if we attack.
What should be done?"
Tàigōng said:
"If you are on the left of the mountain,
urgently prepare the right side of the mountain;
if you are on the right of the mountain,
urgently prepare the left side of the mountain.
If there is a large body of water creating a natural barrier,
and there are no boats or oars,
use a pontoon bridge to ferry our entire army across.
Once across,
quickly widen our road,
so as to facilitate the battlefield.
Use armored chariots as the vanguard and rearguard,
array your strong crossbowmen,
and ensure that all formations are solid.
Obstruct crossroads and valley entrances
with armored chariots.
Set up high banners and flags;
this is called a 'chariot city'.
"Generally, the method of fighting in hazardous terrain
is to use armored chariots as the vanguard,
Large shields will provide defense;
skilled soldiers and strong crossbows
will flank my left and right.
Three thousand men will form a garrison;
they must set up an assault formation,
a convenient place for soldiers to be stationed.
The left army will go to the left,
the right army will go to the right,
the central army will go to the center,
and they will advance with a coordinated attack.
Those who have already fought
will return to their garrisons,
alternating between fighting and resting,
and will not stop until victory is achieved."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent."

*Fēn Bīng* (Dividing the Troops)
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng, saying:
"When a king commands an army,
and the three armies are divided into several locations,
intending to meet for a combined battle,
what should be done regarding agreed oaths, rewards, and punishments?"
Tài Gōng said:
"In the art of employing troops,
the multitude of the Three Armies
must have the variations of division and combination.
The commanding general must first determine the battleground and the battle date,
then issue proclamations to the various generals and officers with a set date,
to attack cities and besiege towns,
each meeting at their designated locations.
Clearly announce the battle day,
with a specific time for each moment.
"The commanding general sets up camp and array,
erects a marker at the camp gate,
clears the road and waits.
When the generals and officers arrive,
check the order of their arrival;
those who arrive before the appointed time are rewarded,
those who arrive late are executed.
If this is done,
then those from near and far will rush to assemble,
the Three Armies will all arrive,
and they will join forces to fight together."
*Wǔ Fēng* (Martial Edge)
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng, saying:
"In the essentials of employing troops,
there must be valiant chariots and swift cavalry,
rushing into battle array and selecting sharp vanguards,
When an opportunity
presents itself, then strike.
How do we determine when it is opportune to strike?"
Tàigōng said:
"Now, those who desire to strike
should carefully observe the enemy's fourteen vulnerabilities.
When these vulnerabilities appear, then strike,
and the enemy will surely be defeated."
King Wǔ asked:
"Can these fourteen vulnerabilities be explained?"
Tàigōng said:
"When the enemy has newly assembled, it is opportune to strike;
when the men and horses have not eaten, it is opportune to strike;
when the weather is unfavorable, it is opportune to strike;
when the terrain is not yet secured, it is opportune to strike;
when they are rushing, it is opportune to strike;
when they are unwary, it is opportune to strike;
when they are exhausted, it is opportune to strike;
when the general is estranged from his soldiers, it is opportune to strike;
when they are crossing a long road, it is opportune to strike;
when they are crossing a river, it is opportune to strike;
when they are pressed for time, it is opportune to strike;
when they are in difficult or narrow passages, it is opportune to strike;
when they are in disarray, it is opportune to strike;
when they are fearful, it is opportune to strike."
《Liàn Shì》
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"What is the way to train soldiers?"
Tài Gōng said:
"In the army, those who are greatly courageous, disregard death, and delight in injury,
gather them into one troop,
called the Soldiers who Brave the Blades.
Those who are full of vigor, bold, brave, strong, and violent,
gather them into one troop,
called the Soldiers who Break the Formation.
Those with unusual appearances, long swords, and who advance in close formation,
gather them into one troop,
called the Soldiers of Courage and Sharpness.
Those who can pull catapults, extend hooks, are strong and powerful, destroy drums and bells, and cut down banners and flags,
gather them into one troop,
called the Soldiers of Courage and Strength.
Those who can climb high, cross great distances, are light-footed, and good at running,
gather them into one troop,
called the Soldiers who Harass the Enemy.
Those ministers of the king who have lost favor and desire to regain merit,
gather them into one troop,
called the Soldiers who Fight to the Death.
Those who are men of a deceased general,
whose sons and younger brothers wish to avenge their general,
gather them into one troop,
called the Soldiers who Dare to Die.
"Those sons-in-law who have been captured by the enemy,
and who wish to conceal their past and achieve fame,
should be gathered into one troop,
named 'The Aspiring Ones' (Lì Dùn zhī Shì).
"Those who are poor and angry,
and who wish to vent their feelings,
should be gathered into one troop,
named 'The Death-Defying Ones' (Bì Sǐ zhī Shì).
"Those who are convicts seeking to be pardoned,
and who wish to escape their shame,
should be gathered into one troop,
named 'The Redeemable Ones' (Xìng Yòng zhī Shì).
"Those who possess outstanding talents
and who are capable of carrying heavy loads over long distances,
should be gathered into one troop,
named 'The Awaiting Orders Ones' (Dài Mìng zhī Shì).
"These are the ways the army should be organized;
this must be understood."
*Teaching War*
King Wǔ asked Grand Duke (Tài Gōng) saying:
"When assembling the masses of the three armies,
how can I ensure that the officers and soldiers are trained in military skills and instructed in the art of war?"
Grand Duke (Tài Gōng) said:
"In commanding the three armies,
there are regulations for the gongs and drums,
which are used to regulate and organize the officers and soldiers.
The general must first clearly inform the officers and soldiers,
reiterating the three commands,
to teach the methods of drilling soldiers, their daily routines, and the changing rules of banners and commands.
Therefore, teach the officers and soldiers:
Have one person learn to fight,
once trained,
combine them into a group of ten;
have ten people learn to fight,
once trained,
combine them into a group of one hundred;
have one hundred people learn to fight,
once trained,
combine them into a group of one thousand;
have one thousand people learn to fight,
once trained,
combine them into a group of ten thousand;
have ten thousand people learn to fight,
once trained,
combine them into the multitude of the three armies;
The method of great battles,
once trained,
combine them into a multitude of one million.
Thus, one can build a great army
and establish power over the world."
King Wǔ
said, "Excellent."
"Equalizing Troops"
King Wǔ asked Tàigōng,
"When fighting with chariots and infantry,
how many infantry soldiers are equivalent to one chariot,
and how many infantry soldiers are equivalent to one chariot?
When fighting with cavalry and infantry,
how many infantry soldiers are equivalent to one horseman,
and how many infantry soldiers are equivalent to one horseman?
When fighting with chariots and cavalry,
how many cavalrymen are equivalent to one chariot,
and how many cavalrymen are equivalent to one chariot?"
Tàigōng said,
"Chariots are the wings of the army,
used to penetrate strong formations, intercept powerful enemies, and block retreating forces.
"Cavalry are the scouts of the army,
used to pursue defeated armies, cut off supply routes, and strike opportunistic raiders.
"Therefore, if chariots and cavalry do not fight together,
then one horseman cannot be equivalent to even one infantry soldier.
When the masses of the three armies form ranks and face each other:
then, in easy battles,
one chariot is equivalent to eighty infantry soldiers,
and eighty infantry soldiers are equivalent to one chariot;
one horseman is equivalent to eight infantry soldiers,
and eight infantry soldiers are equivalent to one horseman;
one chariot is equivalent to ten horsemen,
Ten riders are equivalent to one chariot.
"The method for dangerous battles
is that one chariot is equivalent to forty foot soldiers,
and forty foot soldiers are equivalent to one chariot;
one rider is equivalent to four foot soldiers,
and four foot soldiers are equivalent to one rider;
one chariot is equivalent to six riders,
and six riders are equivalent to one chariot.
Now, chariots and riders are the martial weapons of the army.
Ten chariots can defeat a thousand men,
a hundred chariots can defeat ten thousand men;
ten riders can defeat a hundred men,
a hundred riders can rout a thousand men.
This is the general principle."
Wǔ Wáng 武王 said:
"What are the numbers of officers for chariots and riders, and what are the deployment methods?"
Tàigōng 太公 said:
"Establish the numbers of officers for chariots:
five chariots have one leader,
ten chariots have one officer,
fifty chariots have one commander,
a hundred chariots have one general.
The method for easy battles is that
five chariots form a line,
separated by forty paces,
ten paces to the left and right,
The distance between squads is sixty *bù*.
The method for hazardous battles:
Chariots must follow roads.
Ten chariots form a cluster (*jù*),
Twenty chariots form a garrison (*tún*),
The distance between the front and rear is twenty *bù*,
The distance between left and right is six *bù*,
The distance between squads is thirty-six *bù*.
Five chariots have one leader (*zhǎng*).
The longitudinal and latitudinal distance is two *lǐ*,
Each returns to its original path.
"The number of officials assigned to cavalry:
Five riders have one leader (*zhǎng*),
Ten riders have one officer (*lì*),
One hundred riders have one commander (*shuài*),
Two hundred riders have one general (*jiàng*).
The method for easy battles:
Five riders form a rank (*liè*),
The distance between the front and rear is twenty *bù*,
The distance between left and right is four *bù*,
The distance between squads is fifty *bù*;
For hazardous battles:
The distance between the front and rear is ten *bù*,
The distance between left and right is two *bù*,
The distance between squads is twenty-five *bù*.
Thirty riders form a company (*tún*),
Sixty riders form a group (*bèi*),
Ten riders and one officer,
scattered crisscrossing each other a hundred paces apart,
circling around each returning to their original position."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent."
*Wǔ Chē Shì* (Martial Chariot Warriors)
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng, saying:
"How should chariot warriors be selected?"
Tài Gōng said:
"The method for selecting chariot warriors is to
take those under the age of forty,
who are seven chi and five cun or taller,
who can run fast enough to chase a galloping horse,
and can ride it while galloping,
moving forward, backward, left, right, up, and down in circles,
who can tie and secure flags and banners,
whose strength is sufficient to draw an eight-stone crossbow,
and can shoot forward, backward, left, and right,
all with ease and skill.
They are called martial chariot warriors,
and must be treated with great generosity."
*Wǔ Qí Shì* (Martial Cavalry Warriors)
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng, saying:
"How should cavalry warriors be selected?"
Tài Gōng said:
"The method for selecting cavalry warriors is to
Select those aged forty and below,
who are seven chi and five cun or taller,
robust and swift,
surpassing others,
capable of riding and shooting,
advancing and retreating, turning in all directions,
crossing ditches,
ascending hills,
braving dangers,
traversing vast swamps,
charging strong enemies,
and disrupting large crowds.
These are called "War Cavalrymen,"
and they must be well-treated."
*Chariots*
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"What about war chariots?"
Tài Gōng said,
"Infantry values knowing how to adapt,
chariots value knowing the terrain,
and cavalry values knowing alternative paths and unusual routes.
The three armies have the same name but different uses.
Generally, chariots have ten situations where they are doomed,
and eight situations where they are victorious."
Wǔ Wáng said,
"What are the ten doomed situations?"
Tài Gōng said:
"To go forth and have no way to return is a
*chē*’s (chariot’s) dead ground;
to cross over perilous obstacles and ride against the enemy on a long journey is a
*chē*’s exhausted ground;
when the front is easy and the rear is dangerous,
it is a *chē*'s trapped ground;
to be mired in perilous obstacles and difficult to escape is a
*chē*’s isolated ground;
low-lying, damp marshes and sticky, black clay soil are a
*chē*’s laborious ground;
when the left is dangerous and the right is easy, and going uphill faces a steep slope,
it is a *chē*'s adverse ground;
dense grass across the fields and traversing deep marshes
are a *chē*’s obstructed ground;
when chariots are few and the ground is easy, yet they cannot match the infantry,
it is a *chē*’s defeated ground;
when there are ditches behind, deep water on the left, and steep slopes on the right,
it is a *chē*’s ruined ground;
when it rains day and night,
for ten days without ceasing,
and the roads collapse,
unable to advance forward or retreat backward,
it is a *chē*’s mired ground.
These ten are the *chē*’s dead grounds;
therefore, they are where a clumsy general is captured, and where a wise general is able to avoid."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"What are the 'Eight Victorious Situations'?"
Tàigōng 曰:
"When the enemy's front and rear
have not yet established their battle formation,
immediately assault them;
When banners and flags are in disarray,
and the men and horses move frequently,
immediately assault them;
When soldiers are sometimes forward, sometimes backward,
sometimes left, sometimes right,
immediately assault them;
When the formation is not solid,
and the soldiers look back and forth at each other,
immediately assault them;
When advancing with doubt,
and retreating with fear and timidity,
immediately assault them;
When the entire army is suddenly startled,
and all rise up in agitation,
immediately assault them;
When fighting on difficult terrain,
and unable to disengage by dusk,
immediately assault them;
When marching far and lodging at dusk,
and the entire army is fearful,
immediately assault them.
These eight are the victorious situations for chariots.
If a general is clear about the ten harms and eight victories,
Even though the enemy surrounds (our) perimeter,
with thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of horsemen,
with advance scouts driving ahead and flanking riders darting about,
(we can achieve) "ten thousand battles, surely victorious."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent!"
*War Riders*
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng, saying:
"What about war riders?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Riders have ten advantages and nine disadvantages."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"What are the ten advantages?"
Tài Gōng said:
"When the enemy first arrives,
and the formation has not yet been set,
with the front and rear not connected;
if we trap their front riders,
and strike their left and right flanks,
the enemy will surely flee.
"If the enemy formation is orderly, neat, and secure,
and the soldiers are eager to fight,
our riders should flank them and not leave,
sometimes galloping forward,
sometimes galloping back,
Its swiftness is like the wind,
its violence is like thunder,
daylight becomes darkness,
frequently changing flags,
altering clothing;
such an army can be defeated.
"If the enemy's battle formation is not firm,
and the soldiers do not fight,
press against their front and rear,
hunt down their left and right flanks,
attack them from the wings;
the enemy will surely be afraid.
"If the enemy wants to return to camp at dusk,
and the entire army is fearful and alarmed,
flank them on both sides,
swiftly attack their rear,
press against the openings of their ramparts,
do not let them enter;
the enemy will surely be defeated.
"If the enemy has no dangerous terrain or strongholds to defend,
and advances deeply with long marches,
cut off their supply routes;
the enemy will surely be hungry.
"If the terrain is flat and easy,
and the enemy can be seen on all sides,
trap them with chariots and cavalry;
The enemy will certainly be in disarray.
"When the enemy flees in haste,
and the soldiers scatter in confusion,
some flank them on both sides,
others attack their front and rear,
their general can be captured.
"When the enemy returns at dusk,
with a very large force,
their marching formation will certainly be disordered.
Order my cavalry to form squads of ten,
and companies of one hundred,
chariots to gather in groups of five,
and units of ten,
set up many banners and flags,
mixed with strong crossbows;
some attacking their flanks,
others cutting off their front and rear,
the enemy general can be captured.
These are the ten advantages of cavalry."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"What about the nine defeats?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Generally, when cavalry charges the enemy but cannot break their formation;
and the enemy feigns retreat,
then uses chariots and cavalry to counterattack our rear,
this is a defeat for the cavalry.
"Chasing fleeing enemies and crossing dangerous terrain,
pursuing them relentlessly;
the enemy ambushes us on both sides,
and cuts off our rear;
this is encirclement terrain for cavalry.
"Going forward with no way to return,
entering with no way to exit,
this is called being trapped in a 'celestial well,'
stalled in an 'earth pit';
this is death terrain for cavalry.
"The entry point is narrow,
the exit point is far.
They, being weak, can attack our strong,
they, being few, can attack our many;
this is annihilation terrain for cavalry.
"Large ravines, deep valleys,
dense and luxuriant forests;
this is exhaustion terrain for cavalry.
"Water on the left and right,
a large hill in front,
a high mountain behind;
the three armies battle between two bodies of water,
the enemy occupies both the outer and inner positions;
this is difficult terrain for cavalry.
"The enemy cuts off our supply lines,
Going forth without a means to return
, this is a predicament for cavalry.
"Muddy lowlands and stagnant marshes,
advancing or retreating, the ground is soaked and soggy,
this is a perilous place for cavalry.
"To the left are deep ditches,
to the right are mounds and hillocks,
appearing like flat ground despite the elevation changes,
enticing the enemy to advance or retreat,
this is a trap for cavalry.
"These nine conditions are fatal places for cavalry.
Clear-sighted generals avoid them, while foolish generals fall into defeat because of them."
*Fighting on Foot*
Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng,
"How should infantry fight against chariots and cavalry?"
Tài Gōng said,
"When infantry fights against chariots and cavalry,
they must rely on hills and dangerous terrain.
Long weapons and strong crossbows are placed in the front,
short weapons and weak crossbows are placed in the rear,
alternating firing and stopping.
Even if the enemy's chariots and cavalry arrive in great numbers,
maintain a solid formation and fight swiftly.
Talented soldiers and strong crossbows
should be used to guard our rear."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"I have no hills
, nor any dangerous passes.
When the enemy arrives,
they are both numerous and martial,
their chariots and cavalry flank me on both sides,
and hunt me from front and rear.
My three armies are terrified,
thrown into chaos, defeated, and flee.
What should be done about this?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Order my soldiers to make *xíngmǎ* and wooden caltrops,
place oxen and horses in formations,
and create four *wǔchōngzhèn*.
When you see the enemy's chariots and cavalry approaching,
evenly place the caltrops.
Dig a ditch around the rear,
five *chǐ* wide and deep,
called the 'Destiny Cage'.
Men should advance with *xíngmǎ*,
using the *lánchē* as a barricade,
pushing it forward and backward,
standing it up to form a stronghold.
Skilled soldiers and strong crossbowmen
should be positioned to guard my left and right.
Then order my three armies
to fight fiercely without cease."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent!"
